title: Psalm 80: Restore Us, O God
summary: The people call on the Shepherd of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, to shine forth and save them. Three times a refrain asks God to restore them and make his face shine upon them. At the center of the psalm Israel is pictured as a vine God brought out of Egypt and planted, which once filled the land but now lies broken down and burned, and the people pray for the man at God's right hand.
story: Psalm 80 is the third communal lament in Book III, after Psalms 74 and 79. Where those psalms grieve the fall of Jerusalem, this one focuses on the northern tribes, naming Joseph, Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. It keeps the shepherd image that closed Psalm 79 and turns it into an opening address: the Shepherd of Israel. The psalm's picture of Israel as God's vine, planted with care and then ravaged, becomes one of the Bible's recurring images, taken up by Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and finally by Jesus.
historical:
The heading reads “For the choirmaster. To the tune of “The Lilies of the Covenant.” A Psalm of Asaph.” The tune name, probably the opening words of a known melody, is similar to the tune named in Psalms 45, 60, and 69. For Asaph and his guild, see Psalm 73.

The mention of Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh suggests a setting connected with the northern kingdom of Israel. Ephraim and Manasseh were the sons of Joseph, and with Benjamin they were the descendants of Rachel; in the wilderness these three tribes camped together on the west side of the tabernacle (Numbers 2:18-24). Many scholars date the psalm to the Assyrian campaigns against the northern kingdom in the late eighth century BC, culminating in the fall of Samaria in 722 BC, and some suggest it was prayed in Judah on behalf of the northern tribes. Others place it after the exile, reading the northern names as a way of speaking about all Israel, or earlier still. The psalm doesn't name its enemies, so the setting is inferred rather than stated.
cultural:
The cherubim (verse 1) were winged figures whose carved images stood over the ark of the covenant in the Most Holy Place. God was pictured as enthroned above them, invisible but present (1 Samuel 4:4; 2 Samuel 6:2). To ask him to shine forth is to ask for his presence to be revealed in power. The request that God make his face shine echoes the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26, which asked the LORD to make his face shine on his people and be gracious to them.

Vineyards were central to Israel's economy and culture. A vineyard was protected by a stone wall and a hedge; when the wall was broken, passersby could strip the fruit and wild animals could trample the vines. The wild boar of verse 13 was a known threat in the thickets of the Jordan valley and the hills. The Sea and the River (verse 11) are the Mediterranean and the Euphrates, the ideal boundaries of the land promised to Israel. The bread of tears (verse 5) is a vivid picture of grief so constant it becomes one's daily food.
literary: The psalm is built around a refrain that appears three times (verses 3, 7, and 19), and the name of God grows longer each time: O God, then O God of Hosts, then O LORD God of Hosts. This rising intensity gives the prayer a sense of mounting urgency. The refrains divide the psalm into sections. Verses 1 to 3 call on the Shepherd; verses 4 to 7 lament God's anger; the long central section, verses 8 to 16, tells the story of the vine, from Egypt to its planting, spread, and ruin; verses 17 to 19 pray for the man at God's right hand and end with the refrain. The Hebrew word shuv (return or restore) recurs in the refrain and in verse 14, where the people ask God himself to return.

outline.t: How long will Your anger smolder?
The vine brought out of Egypt
The vine broken down and burned
The man at Your right hand; restore us

doctrines.note: The refrain's prayer, “cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved”, shows that salvation comes from God's favorable presence. Restoration is God's work, not something the people can achieve for themselves.

The vine image recalls God's history with Israel: he brought them out of Egypt, cleared the land, and planted them. The people appeal to that covenant history as the basis for asking God to act again.

Verse 17 prays for the man at God's right hand, the son of man God has raised up. Whether it first referred to Israel, a king, or a coming deliverer, it expresses the hope that God will restore his people through a chosen human figure.

words.note: Shuv, to turn, return, or restore. The refrain asks God to restore the people (verses 3, 7, 19), and in verse 14 they ask God himself to return. The same word often means to repent. Restoration here depends on God's turning toward his people.

Gephen, vine. In verse 8 Israel is the vine God brought out of Egypt. The image recurs in Isaiah 5:1-7, Jeremiah 2:21, Ezekiel 15 and 17, and Hosea 10:1, often describing Israel's failure to bear good fruit. Here the emphasis is on God's care and the vine's present ruin.

Yapha, to shine forth. In verse 1 the people ask the God enthroned above the cherubim to shine forth. The verb is used of God's radiant appearing (Deuteronomy 33:2; Psalm 50:2) and asks for his presence to break through in power and salvation.

Yamin, right hand. It appears in verse 15 (the root Your right hand has planted) and verse 17 (the man at Your right hand). The right hand symbolizes power and favor, and the man at God's right hand is one God has chosen and strengthened.

christ: Jesus took up the vine image directly: “I am the true vine” (John 15:1). Where Israel, the vine of Psalm 80, was broken down and burned, Jesus presents himself as the faithful vine in whom God's people bear fruit. The prayer in verse 17 for the man at God's right hand, the son of man, has been read by Jews and Christians as messianic; the Aramaic Targum on the Psalms interprets the son in verse 15 as the King Messiah. The New Testament presents Jesus as the Son of Man seated at God's right hand (Mark 14:62; Acts 7:56). Jesus is also the good shepherd (John 10:11), the answer to the psalm's opening cry, and in him God's face has shone on his people (2 Corinthians 4:6). The psalm doesn't name the Messiah, but its hopes find their fulfillment in him.
questions: The refrain asks God to make his face shine on his people. What would it look like for God's favor to shine on your life or community now?
Israel is pictured as a vine once flourishing, now broken down. Where do you see a similar story in your own life or church, and how might you pray about it?
Verse 18 promises that if God revives them, they will not turn away. What role does God's reviving work play in our faithfulness?
